Historically, denaturalization is a last resort for fraud and has now been turned into a quota-driven program. What remains unknown is how many monthly referral targets actually become filed cases, and what the court win rate will look like at this scale.

There are about 26 million naturalized U.S. citizens. The 17 cases announced Monday span violent crimes, fraud, and paperwork issues. That's a wider net than what denaturalization has historically been used for.

Denaturalization is a civil or criminal federal court process that requires a judge to strip a naturalized citizen of their citizenship. It's not quick, and it's not supposed to be. Setting monthly numerical quotas is a structural shift in how this power gets used.

New USCIS guidance from December 2025 directs field offices to refer 100–200 denaturalization cases per month to DOJ for FY2026. At that pace, we're looking at potentially 2,400 cases a year, in contrast to Biden's entire four-year term that saw 24 total.

The U.S. averaged about 11 denaturalization cases per year from 1990 to 2017. But on Monday, The DOJ announced 17 new denaturalization cases, it's the largest single-day push in U.S. history and that's on top of 12 cases last month.

What the TIGTA report doesn't tell us: whether any of the 47,000 people whose data was shared actually faced enforcement consequences as a result. The Treasury's own watchdog flagged the problems and the courts flagged them too.

This is what happens when enforcement moves faster than legal process. The IRS has historically been one of the most careful agencies about data privacy, a  reputation that was built deliberately, and it took one memo to start dismantling it.

A federal judge already ruled in February 2026 that the IRS broke the law by disclosing the information of roughly 47,000 people. The IRS's then-acting commissioner resigned. Multiple federal courts have blocked further sharing.
